newsitem.title: KENYA: Spanish aid worker reports "apocalypse" in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Spanish aid worker reports "apocalypse" in Zaire.

text.p: A Spanish aid worker said on Friday an apocalypse was under way in east Zaire and Zairean colleagues who fled fighting had reported by radio Rwandan refugees dying in their thousands from thirst and poisonous gases on a lava field.
Fernando Rodriguez of Medecins du Monde (Doctors of the World) told Reuters eastern Zaire, which he escaped on Wednesday, was in virtual mayhem with armed bands looting villages, camps and homes.
"Once they left Kahindo camp, we heard Zairean NGO workers trying to report by radio to Goma they had no water. Many people were dying of gas, gas you can't smell from the lava," he said.
"They were dying in their thousands. It was an apocalypse."
"We could see them through the binoculars on the lava field but we couldn't see them dying. It was too far," said Rodriguez, who hid for days in a Belgian coffee manager's home near Kahindo.
"We could see them in the distance crossing the lava field in different groups. Some headed for the volcano, some headed for the forest. All 175,000 left Kahindo camp in three groups," he said.
Asked about the slow organisation of any international force to protect aid operations, Rodriguez said: "We cannot leave them."
"Sure there are some guilty people, some genocide killers, among the Rwandan refugees but 95 percent of them are innocent and did nothing wrong but to be born Hutus. They are the ones dying.

"Soldiers and wrong ones are the ones most likely to survive. The innocent, women, children and the old are first to die. They should get aid as soon as possible. Every minute counts in the lava fields.
"It is shocking everyone in Nairobi is discussing things in a very civilised manner and every minute people are dying," he said.
Some of the 1.1 million Hutu Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire refuse to go home because they took part in the 1994 genocide.
Rodriguez, 32 and from Madrid, said armed gangs of Rwandans broke into all warehouses in Katale and Kahindo camps with a total population of 314,000 and stripped them bare as refugees left.

"We were amazed to see some of them climb up the mountains. We saw the camp fires at night," he added. He said mayday radio calls from the 32 Zairean aid workers who left with the refugees stopped as batteries died.
He said armed groups of Zairean soldiers from various army units, exiled Rwandan Hutu militiamen and Rwandan Hutu refugees were rampaging in the region, looting camps and Zairean villages.
He said former Rwandan Hutu soldiers twice threatened to execute him and other foreign aid workers -- with a machinegun and then with a hand grenade -- and told them to say their prayers.

But they were first distracted when one former soldier found some money on a woman and then fled when a mob approached to loot the house. He said three waves of about 100 refugees armed with machetes and bars picked the house where they were hiding clean.
He said Zairean troops paid by the U.N. refugee agency to guard the camps fled and stole all the aid workers' vehicles.
Rodriguez said he, two Belgians and two Italians walked barefoot for 25 km (16 miles) to escape to reach Spanish nuns in Rubari village, from where rebels allowed them to reach Uganda.
He reported deserted villages on a 35-km (22-mile) stretch of road between Rutshuru north of Goma and the Ugandan border.

An aid worker for Action for Churches Together (ACT) earlier told a Nairobi meeting that a survey by plane this week showed a large concentration of people in the jungle between the Zairean towns of Hombo and Walikale.
He said the mixture of Rwandan refugees and displaced Zaireans had stayed in the jungle for about three weeks and looked "in very bad condition" and were extremely tense and robbing each other.
A three-week rebel offensive in eastern Zaire has uprooted tens of thousands of Zaireans and large numbers of 1.1 million Rwandan refugees and 200,000 Burundian refugees in the region.
